crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: FAIR Data
children.blurb: FAIR Data is a set of guiding principles for making research data Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable, published in 2016 and now widely adopted across research funders, journals and repositories.

children.name: Metadata and Ontologies
children.blurb: Metadata and ontologies in research data and repositories cover the structured descriptions that make data, papers, models, and tools discoverable and the formal vocabularies that give those descriptions shared meaning.

children.name: Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data
children.blurb: Federated sharing of sensitive data covers arrangements where two or more organisations analyse data that cannot be pooled in one place, such as patient records, genomic sequences, financial transactions or personal device data.

children.name: Institutional Knowledge Graphs
children.blurb: Institutional knowledge graphs represent the entities an organization cares about, such as people, projects, publications, datasets, instruments, and administrative units, and the relationships among them.

children.name: Long-Term Digital Preservation
children.blurb: Long-term digital preservation is the work of keeping digital objects usable, understandable, and trustworthy over decades, across changes in hardware, software, formats, and organizations.

sections.body: Research data and repositories covers the machinery that makes scientific data findable, understandable, shareable and durable over decades. In practice, artificial intelligence is being used to generate metadata automatically from papers and datasets, to align ontologies across disciplines, to match queries to relevant records, and to detect inconsistencies in large collections. The site's own library illustrates the scale involved, with 295 research papers, 14104 claims extracted from research works, 804 scientific models and 850 AI tools catalogued and linked back to original sources rather than to a search tool. These systems are less about discovery of new science and more about keeping the record of science usable.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Metadata extraction and ontology alignment work well on well structured domains such as genomics and materials science, where vocabularies are mature and formats are stable. Federated sharing of sensitive data is technically feasible through methods like differential privacy and secure computation, but it remains slow in practice because governance, consent and institutional policy lag behind the tooling. Long term preservation is the weakest area, since formats, storage media and funding cycles all change faster than the timescales preservation demands. Institutional knowledge graphs are promising but often incomplete, and their quality depends on curation that few institutions fund continuously. The honest limit is that no automated system has removed the need for human judgement about what a dataset means and whether it should be reused.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader should start with FAIR Data for the principles that shape everything else, then move to Metadata and Ontologies for the vocabularies and schemas that make those principles operational. Federated Sharing of Sensitive Data addresses the harder case where records cannot simply be copied, covering the technical and governance arrangements that allow analysis without central pooling. Institutional Knowledge Graphs shows how an organisation connects its own people, projects, datasets and outputs into a queryable structure, which is where much of the practical AI work now sits. Long-Term Digital Preservation closes the section by asking what survives when the software, the storage and the institution itself change, and it is the page to read if durability rather than access is the concern.
